The addition of ALMA to this study results in an improvement of the SED at high redshift (i.e, at 3.1 ≤ z ≤ 5.0).

findings_qualitative.value: The mean mass-weighted dust temperature of main sequence galaxies evolves linearly with redshift up to z ~ 5 with no apparent correlation with stellar mass.

evidence.quote: The mean Tdust of MS galaxies evolves linearly with redshift, with no apparent correlation with M⋆.

findings_qualitative.value: The SFR-M* main sequence has a slope close to unity at low masses with a bending at the high-mass end that becomes more prominent at z < 2.

evidence.quote: We confirm that the SFR-M⋆ star formation main sequence (MS) follows a linear evolution with a slope close to unity with a bending at the high-mass end at z < 2.

findings_qualitative.value: Massive galaxies (M* >= 10^10 Msun) account for more than 70% of the total cosmic SFR density across all redshifts up to z ~ 5, while lower-mass galaxies (M* <= 10^10 Msun) have a roughly constant contribution.

evidence.quote: We show that, up to z ∼ 5, massive galaxies (i.e. M⋆ ≥ 1010 M⊙ ) account for most of the total SFR density (ρSFR ), while the contribution of lower-mass galaxies (i.e. M⋆ ≤ 1010 M⊙ ) is rather constant.
We again observe that massive galaxies (i.e. log10 (M⋆/M⊙) > 10) dominate the total ρSFR at all redshifts (i.e. they account for more than 70%).

findings_qualitative.value: In the TNG100 cosmological simulation, massive galaxies do not form enough stars around cosmic noon (z ~ 2) and have lower gas fractions than observed, possibly due to overly efficient AGN feedback.

evidence.quote: We find that TNG100 exhibits a noticeable difference in the evolution of the CSFH, that is, the marked evolution of massive galaxies found in the observations appears to be smoothed in the simulation, possibly due to feedback that is too efficient.

We conclude that the mechanisms used to regulate star formation (in particular feedback from AGNs) are possibly too strong in this simulation, namely too efficient at producing a drop in the gas content in massive galaxies.

findings_qualitative.value: High-redshift galaxies (z = 3-5) exhibit a stronger star formation efficiency (shorter depletion time) at fixed gas surface density compared to low-redshift galaxies.

evidence.quote: Finally, we find hints that the star formation efficiency of distant galaxies (z = 3–5) is stronger (shorter depletion time) as compared to low-redshift galaxies.
Overall, even though the evolution of the SFE with redshift is not well constrained, this study suggests that galaxies at high-redshift form stars more efficiently at a fixed gas surface density.

claims.hypothesis: The dust temperature of main sequence galaxies evolves linearly with redshift up to z ~ 5 and does not depend on stellar mass at fixed redshift.
claims.experiment: Fit Schreiber et al. (2018) dust SED templates to mean-stacked Spitzer, Herschel, and ALMA photometry across bins of stellar mass and redshift from z = 0.1 to 5.0.
claims.result: T_dust shows no significant dependence on M* at fixed redshift and follows the linear relation T_dust [K] = 34.20(+0.14/-0.15) + 5.06(+0.03/-0.03)(z - 2).
claims.finding: The mean dust temperature of main sequence galaxies is mainly determined by redshift, evolving linearly up to z = 5 independently of stellar mass.

evidence.quote: It seems that, overall, the Tdust of a main sequence galaxy is mainly determined by its redshift, independently of its M⋆ (see also Magdis et al. 2012; Magnelli et al. 2014).

claims.hypothesis: Massive galaxies (M* >= 10^10 Msun) dominate the cosmic star formation rate density (rho_SFR) and cosmic gas density (rho_gas) up to z ~ 5, while lower-mass galaxies provide a roughly constant contribution.
claims.experiment: Combine the stacked main sequence SFR and gas mass relations with the Davidzon et al. (2017) stellar mass functions and Wang et al. (2019) H-dropout sample, integrating down to M* = 3 x 10^9 Msun.
claims.result: Galaxies with M* > 10^10 Msun account for >70% of the total rho_SFR at all redshifts (with 10.5 <= log10(M*/Msun) <= 11.25 accounting for >55% at z = 2), whereas rho_SFR for M* < 10^10 Msun remains roughly constant around log10(rho_SFR) ~ -1.6 to -1.9.
claims.finding: Massive galaxies drive the rise and fall of the cosmic star formation history and peak at cosmic noon, while low-mass galaxies contribute a nearly constant SFR and gas density over cosmic time.

evidence.quote: We again observe that massive galaxies (i.e. log10 (M⋆/M⊙) > 10) dominate the total ρSFR at all redshifts (i.e. they account for more than 70%).
We can see the same kind of features as for the evolution of ρ SFR : a rise and fall with redshift with a maximum around

claims.hypothesis: H-dropout (HST-dark) galaxies dominate the cosmic star formation rate density among the most massive galaxies at z > 3.
claims.experiment: Add the ALMA-detected H-dropout sample from Wang et al. (2019) to the mass-complete H-band selected sample and compute their relative contribution to rho_SFR.
claims.result: H-dropouts account for 13% of the total cosmic SFR density at z = 4-6 and ~23% of the stars formed in massive galaxies (M* >= 10^10.3 Msun).
claims.finding: H-dropout galaxies make a significant (~23%) but not dominant contribution to the SFR density of massive galaxies at z > 3 when compared against a stellar-mass-complete sample rather than UV-selected LBGs.

evidence.loc: 8.1. Cosmic densities of star formation and gas density as a function of stellar mass
evidence.quote: We note that H-dropout galaxies account for ∼23% of the stars formed in massive galaxies (i.e. M⋆ ≥ 1010.3 M⊙). This is a large contribution but not a dominant one, as opposed to the claim of Wang et al. (2019) that H-dropouts dominate the SFR density in the most massive galaxies.

claims.hypothesis: The TNG100 cosmological simulation reproduces the observed stellar-mass-dependent contributions to the cosmic star formation rate density.
claims.experiment: Integrate the SFR of galaxies in TNG100 down to M* = 3 x 10^9 Msun split into M* > 10^10 Msun and M* < 10^10 Msun, and compare gas fractions and SFRs with the observational stacking results.
claims.result: In TNG100, massive galaxies (M* > 10^10 Msun) contribute only ~50% of the observed rho_SFR at z = 2, the ratio rho_SFR(M*>10^10)/rho_SFR(M*<10^10) decreases monotonically with z instead of peaking at ~5.6 at z ~ 1.7, and f_gas < 15% for M* > 10^10 Msun.
claims.finding: TNG100 fails to reproduce the stellar-mass-dependent evolution of the CSFH because massive galaxies are overly gas-depleted and quenched too early, likely due to overly efficient AGN feedback.

evidence.quote: The disparities between the two total ρSFR trends can be almost exclusively associated with the contribution of massive galaxies being off in the TNG100 simulation.

We conclude that the mechanisms used to regulate star formation (in particular feedback from AGNs) are possibly too strong in this simulation, namely too efficient at producing a drop in the gas content in massive galaxies.

claims.hypothesis: Star formation efficiency (SFE) is universal across redshift and depends only on the available gas reservoir via a redshift-invariant Kennicutt-Schmidt relation.
claims.experiment: Compare SFE and SFE / M_gas^(N-1) across redshift and stellar mass bins using the fitted Kennicutt-Schmidt slope N = 1.18 (and N = 1.29 for Scoville et al. 2016 gas masses).
claims.result: At z > 2, the normalisation of SFE / M_gas^(N-1) increases by a factor of ~3 between z ~ 2 and z ~ 4.3, and between z = 1.15 and z = 2 for 10.5 <= log10(M*/Msun) <= 11 an intrinsic SFE increase of a factor ~2.3 is found beyond the gas mass increase.
claims.finding: Distant galaxies (z = 3-5) convert gas into stars more efficiently at a fixed gas surface density than low-redshift galaxies, indicating an intrinsic redshift evolution of the SFE.

evidence.quote: this study suggests that galaxies at high-redshift form stars more efficiently at a fixed gas surface density.

Overall, even though the evolution of the SFE with redshift is not well constrained, this study suggests that galaxies at high-redshift form stars more efficiently at a fixed gas surface density. This excess cannot be explained by a universal Kennicutt-Schmidt relation nor SFE over all redshifts.

why_this_data.value: Combining deep Herschel surveys in four fields with the blind 1.13 mm GOODS-ALMA survey accounts for dust attenuation and reaches lower stellar masses and higher redshifts (up to z ~ 5) while constraining the FIR SED peak.

evidence.quote: Attenuation by dust is accounted for thanks to the combination of deep surveys by Herschel and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter array (ALMA).

However, the addition of ALMA measurements to Herschel using stacking has not been carried out yet. The reason is that this requires access to an extensive study programme on ALMA. This has only recently been possible thanks to blind surveys such as the GOODS-ALMA survey (Franco et al. 2018, 2020; Gómez-Guijarro et al. 2022a).

why_this_method.value: Stellar-mass selection and mean stacking avoid uncertain extrapolations of the IR luminosity function (which is polluted by starbursts), avoid non-linear median stacking biases, and allow recovery of total flux for faint galaxy populations; the S18 SED library has few free parameters suited for sparse FIR sampling; the MZR gas mass method accounts for metallicity variations with stellar mass.

evidence.quote: In order to avoid uncertain extrapolations of the infrared luminosity function, which is often polluted by the contribution of starbursts, we base our analysis on stellar mass.
the mean stack gives us access to the total flux in the stack, which we currently miss to infer
We favoured the present method because it takes into account the variation of metallicity and the associated change in dust-to-gas ratio as a function of stellar mass.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Median stacking (rejected in favour of mean stacking because median is non-linear and introduces systematic biases at low S/N or for skewed flux distributions)

evidence.quote: We choose to use mean stacking for our work, rather than median stacking.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Stacking undetected sources on residual maps separately from detected sources (rejected in favour of stacking all sources directly on the original maps for consistency and to avoid biases)

evidence.quote: Following S15, we have therefore chosen to treat detected and undetected sources in the same way for consistency (i.e. directly from the image and not from the residual).

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Stacking ALMA data in the uv plane (rejected in favour of image-plane stacking to save computing time after tests showed only a 10% difference)

evidence.quote: We decided not to stack directly in the uv plane but in the image plane in order to save computing time as this should not impact the results of this study.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Fitting SEDs directly with Draine & Li (2007) / Draine et al. (2014) models (rejected as primary fit in favour of Schreiber et al. 2018 templates because Draine & Li has too many free parameters for sparse high-z/low-mass FIR data)

evidence.quote: Because we do not have many points on the FIR at low M⋆ and high redshifts, we used the library from Schreiber et al. (2018, hereafter S18), which is well suited for our study given its small number of free parameters. Choosing a model with more parameters, such as Draine & Li (2007) and Draine et al. (2014), would imply fixing parameters on some bins.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Alternative gas mass derivations: Leroy et al. (2011) delta_GDR, Mannucci et al. (2010) FMR metallicity, Galliano et al. (2021) amorphous carbon dust model, and using only Scoville et al. (2016) RJ continuum method (tested and compared; MZR + Magdis et al. 2012 + Draine & Li 2007 scale adopted as baseline)

evidence.quote: We note that by using the δGDR relation of Leroy et al. (2011), instead of Magdis et al. (2012), would not change our conclusions
We produced a version of our analysis using the same method for consistency check, it is presented in Appendix B.

limitations_admitted.value: H-band selection may become a less robust proxy for stellar mass at z > 3 and misses H-dropout galaxies (which are added a posteriori from Wang et al. 2019).

evidence.quote: H-dropout galaxies are by definition not included in these samples, as they are not detected in H-band. However, we used the sample from Wang et al. (2019) to add and discuss their impact in any necessary analyses.
This hypothesis may however become less robust at high redshifts

limitations_admitted.value: Optical-to-mm centroid offsets and high angular resolution cause the ALMA stacked images to be extended on scales larger than the ALMA PSF.

evidence.quote: Due to the high angular resolution of the ALMA data, and to possible small offsets between the optical centroids (on which our stack positions are based) and millimetre centroids, the stacked images are extended on scales larger than that of the ALMA PSF.

limitations_admitted.value: Very massive galaxies (M* > 2-3 x 10^11 Msun) at z > 3 cannot be probed because they are extremely rare.

evidence.loc: 5.2. The main sequence of star-forming galaxies
evidence.quote: Another possibility is that the bending still occurs at high redshifts, but only for very high-mass galaxies (M⋆ > 2 − 3 × 1011 M⊙), which we could not probe with this study because they are extremely rare.

limitations_admitted.value: Total gas masses derived from dust at z < 0.4 cannot be used for H2 because the atomic gas (HI) content is not probed.

evidence.quote: Therefore, we decided not to consider our Mgas for z < 0.4 (i.e. our first redshift bin), as we could not probe the HI content of the galaxy at these redshifts.

limitations_admitted.value: Galaxy morphology and effective radii Re are not directly measured in this study, preventing direct fitting of the size term in the gas scaling relation and requiring literature Re(z, M*) relations for the Kennicutt-Schmidt analysis.

evidence.quote: And we do not explore the morphology of galaxies in this study, which makes it impossible to probe the term Eµ, which compares the effective radius of galaxies (Re) to the mean effective radius of the star forming population Re 0.
We do not probe Re in this study, thus, we chose to use Re(z, M⋆), for galaxies with M⋆ ≥ 1010, from Wang et al. (2022).

limitations_admitted.value: The low stellar mass and high redshift regime of the cosmic gas mass density relies on uncertain extrapolations and is sensitive to the functional form chosen to fit M_gas.

evidence.loc: 7. Cosmic evolution of the gas mass density
evidence.quote: The latter part is a potential weakness of all studies including ours, since the low stellar mass – high redshift of the cosmic gas mass density range relies on rather uncertain extrapolations.

referee_caveats_inferred: ALMA 1.13 mm coverage is only available in a 69 arcmin^2 sub-region of GOODS-South (8,659 galaxies out of 128,952 total across 1,077 arcmin^2), so the ALMA stacked photometry probes ~1/15th the volume and sample size of the Herschel stacks and is more susceptible to cosmic variance.

In the two lowest-mass high-z bins (10.0 <= log10(M*) <= 10.5 at 3.1 <= z <= 3.9 and 3.9 <= z <= 5.0), only the single ALMA 1.13 mm point is detected, requiring T_dust to be restricted to the S18 evolution +- 10 K for L_IR and switching from the MZR dust-to-gas method to the Scoville et al. (2016) single-band calibration for M_gas.

The Kennicutt-Schmidt and SFE evolution conclusions at z > 3 depend on assumed average effective radii Re(z, M*) taken from Wang et al. (2022) rather than size measurements of the stacked galaxies themselves.
